cls: Live attenuated viral vaccine (oral active immunization)
pharm: Active immunizing agent / rotavirus gastroenteritis prevention
quick: Oral administration: 3 doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age (Rotavac/Rotasiil/Rotateq) or 2 doses at 6 and 10 weeks (Rotarix)
STRICTLY ORAL — NEVER INJECT. Discard if inadvertently given parenterally
Dose 1 by 12-15 weeks of age; final dose strictly completed by 8 months (32 weeks) of age
History of intussusception or uncorrected congenital GI malformation; severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
Educate parents to report signs of intussusception (severe colicky abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bloody/currant-jelly stools)
summary: Rotavirus vaccine is a live attenuated oral viral vaccine (monovalent human G1P[8], pentavalent human-bovine reassortant G1-G4+P[8], or neonatal strain 116E) designed for the active immunization of infants against severe dehydrating rotavirus diarrhea and gastroenteritis. It is administered strictly orally in a 2- or 3-dose schedule beginning at 6 weeks of age. The maximum age for the first dose is 15 weeks, and the full series must be completed by 8 months (32 weeks) of age due to age-related baseline risk of intussusception.
indications: Active immunization of infants from 6 weeks of age for the prevention of rotavirus gastroenteritis caused by prevalent viral serotypes
Universal inclusion in national and global infant immunization schedules to reduce childhood diarrheal morbidity and mortality

dosage.d: Oral liquid or reconstituted drops: 1 dose at 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks of age
dosage.n: First dose should be given between 6 and 15 weeks of age. Series must be completed by 32 weeks (8 months).

dosage.d: 1 oral dose at 6 weeks and 10 weeks of age
dosage.n: Series must be completed by 24 weeks of age.

admin: Administer STRICTLY BY THE ORAL ROUTE. Never inject intramuscularly, subcutaneously, or intravenously.
If an infant spits out or regurgitates most of a dose, a single replacement dose may be considered at the same visit, although official WHO guidance allows continuing the schedule without repeating.
Breastfeeding before or after vaccination does not significantly impair immune response; feeding need not be restricted.
Maintain cold chain: store between 2°C and 8°C.
moa: The live attenuated rotavirus replicates in the small intestinal mucosa, mimicking natural subclinical infection. It induces local mucosal secretory IgA antibodies in the gut and circulating neutralizing serum IgG antibodies against the viral outer capsid VP4 (P-type) and VP7 (G-type) proteins, conferring high-grade clinical protection against moderate to severe dehydrating rotavirus enteritis.

absolute: Uncorrected congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract predisposing to intussusception (e.g., Meckel diverticulum)
Severe anaphylactic hypersensitivity to a previous dose of rotavirus vaccine
relative: Moderate to severe acute gastroenteritis or vomiting/diarrhea (defer until resolved to ensure adequate intestinal retention)
Acute moderate or severe febrile illness
monitor: Intussusception symptoms within 1 to 21 days post-vaccination (peak risk in days 1 to 7): sudden episodic paroxysmal inconsolable crying, legs pulled to abdomen, bilious vomiting, lethargy, red 'currant-jelly' stool
Mild transient irritability, low-grade fever, loose stools

lact: Not applicable to maternal use. Breastfed infants can receive the vaccine normally.
serious_se: Intussusception (very rare, estimated ~1 to 5 excess cases per 100,000 vaccinated infants, predominantly within 7 days after dose 1 or 2)
Vaccine-strain viral shedding and transmission (wash hands thoroughly after diaper changes)
monitoring: Counsel parents explicitly on the symptoms of intussusception and advise immediate emergency pediatric evaluation if severe episodic crying, bilious vomiting, or bloody stools occur
